title: UNH football can't slow Sacred Heart rushing attack in 20-13 conference loss - Yahoo Sports
content: FAIRFIELD, Conn. – Sacred Heart University leaned on a powerful rushing attack, running 59 times for 243 yards and defeated the University of New Hampshire, 20-13, in a Coastal Athletic Association (CAA) football game Saturday, Sept. 26. The Wildcats fell to 1-4 overall and 0-2 in conference play, while Sacred Heart improved to 1-3 overall and 1-2 in the CAA. Joquez Smith paced the UNH offense with a game-high 107 rushing yards on 18 carries. Myles Thomason added 74 yards on 11 carries, including a 49-yard touchdown run. Quarterback Brooks Bentley completed 11 of 19 passes for 81 yards, with his longest completion a 24-yard connection to tight end Colby Ramshaw. Defensively, Trevor Barry recorded a career-high 16 tackles, while Cohen Cook added a personal-best 15 tackles. Matthew Sopp contributed a career-high seven tackles and forced a fumble that was recovered by Cook. Ethan Aghakhan also posted a personal-best seven tackles. UNH returns home Saturday, Oct. 3, to host Elon University in a CAA matchup scheduled for a 1 p.m. kickoff. title: What Do History Majors Do? - University of New Hampshire
content: Are you fascinated with how things used to be and what that means for us now? History is the study of the past and how that knowledge can inform the present and the future. This is a broad degree program, allowing you to focus on a particular country, region, time period, or aspect of human culture that interests you, such as religion, science, or cultural movements. You’ll develop the skills in critical reading and writing that form the basis of a solid liberal arts education and prepare you for a wide range of careers, as well as graduate or professional school. Meet William Kirkpatrick '26, a history major from Eliot, Maine, who has found a close community on the UNH campus, with plenty of room to explore by studying how dinosaur bones may have influenced Greek mythology and by studying abroad in Turkey. William Kirkpatrick: I chose UNH because the campus has the appeal of the beautiful small schools of New England while providing enough opportunities, classes, and people to feel like a significant step up from my small Maine high school. Growing up with two parents who worked at UNH, I also had the opportunity to meet some of the professors, faculty, and staff, all of whom were extremely kind and welcoming. It seemed like an easy choice. My favorite thing about COLA is that almost every class I took during my first three years allowed me to explore topics I had never considered before. Coming in my first year, I certainly didn't think I would write a final paper two years later comparing Odysseus in Homer's "The Odyssey" to Mad Max. I can't think of another college that would actively encourage such ambitions. "Almost every class I took during my first three years allowed me to explore topics I had never considered before." I love the history department because of the many subjects it offers. One class will have me writing about medieval hunting practices, and the next will provide the opportunity to present about why dinosaur bones have heavily influenced Greek mythology. I believe, above all, that my liberal arts education has given me the ability to think critically and present my thoughts in a convincing manner after considering the presented material. Paraphrasing Professor Gregory McMahon, a liberal arts education is a lesson in persuasion, critical thinking, and independence presented in the most fascinating way possible. I agree! "I believe, above all, that my liberal arts education has given me the ability to think critically and present my thoughts in a convincing manner." My most impactful professors are both Professor Gregory McMahon and Professor David Bachrach. During my first semester freshman year, Professor Bachrach taught me how to write like a historian and encouraged me to reach out to him with drafts of all my papers. I still refer to some of my papers from that year for format and grammar. Then, in my sophomore year, Professor McMahon helped me understand how fun it is to create new ideas based on ancient sources and supported me when I would come to him with frankly crazy ideas for papers. Professor McMahon sent me to study abroad on his archaeological dig in Turkey this summer. I never took people who said that studying abroad would change your life seriously, because how could it? However, my time in Turkey is one of the highlights of my college experience and probably my life. It's such a vastly different culture from ours, but I fit right in since everyone I met treated me as if they had known me their whole life. In addition to the amazing Turkish culture, getting to see, touch, and excavate the artifacts that I've spent so much of my college career reading about, analyzing, and writing about is a once-in-a-lifetime experience that I can hopefully turn into a twice-in-a-lifetime experience in the near future. "I never took people who said that studying abroad would change your life seriously, because how could it? However, my time in Turkey is one of the highlights of my college experience and probably my life." I received the Trustee's Scholarship coming in my freshman year. This scholarship allowed me to free up money to study abroad in Turkey this summer. I will be forever grateful that UNH allowed me the opportunity to experience Turkish culture from a perspective that many people are not afforded. There are two pieces of advice I would give my freshman self. The first is to explore the campus earlier. There are many cool areas, such as College Woods, the Fishbowl, and the tennis courts, that I never really used until later on. UNH is meant to be explored, and everyone has their favorite spot on campus to study and hang out. The second piece is to study abroad earlier. If I had the chance to go on a second trip before graduation, I would have taken it immediately. I was originally scared that I would feel alone, homesick, and out of place, but I found the opposite was true. There will never be another opportunity to experience international culture like that offered in college, so why not take it? I have found a sense of community within my friend group. Most of us met during the "Become the Roar" tradition during orientation, and we have stayed very close friends throughout all four years. My freshman year roommate is still my best friend, and all of us shared an eight-person suite in Mills Hall during my sophomore year. One thing people might be surprised to learn about me is that during the summers, I work as a groundskeeper for my local cemetery. After someone learns this, I am immediately asked if I bury the people, too, which, yes, I do. However, I am hopefully far from the cemetery groundskeeper stereotype. title: Vermonters back 2nd-home tax, divided on school consolidation, safe injection sites, according to UNH poll - WCAX
content:
BURLINGTON, Vt. (WCAX) - Vermonters strongly support placing a new tax on second homes, but are divided on school consolidation and safe injection sites, according to a new poll by the University of New Hampshire Survey Center. In the poll, 78% of respondents say they support a tax on homes that are not the primary residence of property owners, while 15% oppose it. Legislation with bipartisan backing is expected to be taken up by the Legislature next year. School consolidation dominated the last biennium, with lawmakers pulling back from mandatory mergers. But nearly half of Vermonters continue to favor school district consolidation, even if that leads to school closures. The poll found 49% support the idea of lowering education costs, while 39% are opposed. Harm reduction methods, like safe injection sites, have also been a focal point in Burlington. The survey shows Vermonters at large are divided over opening a site where drug use happens under the supervision of medical professionals, with 39% in favor and 43% opposed. title: Latest poll shows Gov. Phil Scott and Amanda Janoo in tightest race in a decade - VTDigger
content:
Prepare for Vermont’s Nov. 3 general election with VTDigger’s 2026 Election Guide. Get the latest reporting from towns across Vermont delivered each morning in Daily Digger, our free newsletter. A Vermont election poll on the upcoming governor’s race suggests it might be the closest in a decade. The most recent University of New Hampshire Green Mountain State Poll released this week reported that 49% of Vermonters support Amanda Janoo in the November election, while 43% support incumbent Gov. Phil Scott. The 6% margin led UNH pollsters to declare the Governor’s race a “statistical tie.” In a July poll released by the same group, Scott led Janoo by 15% meaning the recent numbers account for a 21-point swing. The poll also reported former Democratic Lieutenant Governor Molly Gray leading Republican incumbent John Rodgers 54% to 35% in the lieutenant governor race. U.S. Rep. Becca Balint, D-Vt., comfortably leads the state’s one congressional race with a 35% margin against Republican nominee Gerald Malloy. Scott’s approval rating, according to the poll, has fallen 5% since July, sitting at 47%. In the October 2025 Green Mountain State Poll, the incumbent’s approval rating was 61% with a majority of Vermonters supporting a reelection bid. In a press release Thursday, Scott’s campaign manager Dustin Degree criticized UNH’s polling methods, specifically its partisan split. Some 60% of those surveyed self-identified as Democrats, 31% as Republicans and 9% as Independent. Scott has historically held significant bipartisan support, but after a series of vetos on progressive bills, some Vermonters have said they’re looking for change. Degree cited UNH’s 2024 poll, which predicted a 28% margin of victory for Scott, who went on to win reelection by more than 50%. He called Thursday’s poll “statistical malpractice.” “The good news is, besides exciting headlines and political posturing, outlier polls don’t matter,” the press release reads. “Election Day does.” Janoo’s grassroots campaign was successful in the primary election. She defeated Aly Richards by just over 3%. Janoo, an economist and first-time political candidate, described her democratic primary election victory as a “long-shot.”  In a press release, Janoo’s team wrote that the poll’s results reflected what they had heard “on the ground every day.” “Vermonters are tired of a status quo that’s failing us,” the press release said. “We’re tired of managed decline for our state. We’re looking for hope and leadership that believes in Vermont. Together, we can not only win this election, but build a better future.” Thursday’s poll teed up November’s general election, based on 882 survey responses collected last week. The data were weighted based on demographic information from the U.S. Census and 2024 election results, according to the survey. VTDigger's intern.

title: UNH Researcher Lends Expertise to Help Outline Priorities in U.S. Climate Assessment - University of New Hampshire
content: Serita Frey, professor of natural resources and the environment at UNH, is a co-author of the commentary “Research priorities for robust climate assessments in the United States.” The paper brings together 175 authors across the United States to outline research priorities that can inform future national, regional, local, sectoral and topical climate assessments. The commentary was published in the journals Earth’s Future and Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society. It is the first paper in the U.S. Climate Collection: Informing Assessment of Risks and Solutions—a joint special collection of the American Geophysical Union and the American Meteorological Society that will publish U.S.-focused climate assessment science and research synthesis papers that can inform future national and sub-national assessments. Frey contributed to the commentary through leading the section on forests which identifies key research priorities for understanding how U.S. forests are responding to climate change, including the effects of warming, drought, wildfire, pests, and other disturbances. It also highlights the need to better quantify the role of forests in carbon storage and climate mitigation, while supporting biodiversity and ecosystem services. “As climate risks intensify, forests will play an increasingly important role in carbon storage, biodiversity conservation, and community resilience," says Frey. “This paper identifies key research priorities needed to ensure that future climate assessments capture both the vulnerabilities of forests and their potential to help address climate change.” The commentary identifies assessment opportunities and research needs across planetary-scale systems, environmental settings, economic sectors, U.S. regions and U.S. international interests. Across these areas, the authors identify several cross-cutting priorities for research synthesis, including how greenhouse gas emissions continue to alter and amplify climate hazards; how compounding extremes and cascading risks are straining legacy policies, infrastructure, and institutions; how social systems shape both climate impacts and responses; and how future assessments should evaluate mitigation, adaptation, disaster management, climate interventions and resilience planning and implementation decisions as a climate action portfolio. Scientific assessments synthesize complex bodies of evidence so households, communities, businesses, institutions and governments can make informed decisions as climate hazards intensify. The most recent U.S. National Climate Assessment was published in 2023; scientific understanding has advanced since then, and climate assessments are continuing by states, localities and businesses. The commentary argues that the pace of assessment and the integration of science with decision-making must accelerate as climate impacts continue to grow. title: UNH Vs. HUM: Which Insurer Stock Has More Upside After CMS Reverses Wall Street’s Biggest Medicare Rate Fear? - Stocktwits
content: Shares of UnitedHealth, Inc. (UNH) and Humana, Inc. (HUM) are back in the spotlight on Tuesday after the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) lifted Medicare Advantage payment rates for 2027, with Wall Street estimates pointing to a clear frontrunner. UNH stock rose 8% in extended trading, while HUM stock gained 11%. Over the past year, however, UNH has fallen about 45% and HUM nearly 27%, with both stocks underperforming the broader Health Care Select Sector SPDR Fund (XLV), which climbed 10% over the same period. The CMS finalized a 2.48% increase in Medicare Advantage payment rates for 2027, up from the January proposal that kept rates roughly flat and wiped out nearly $100 billion in market value across major insurers. The updated policy is expected to add more than $13 billion in additional funding to Medicare Advantage plans next year, the CMS said. With the policy overhang removed, attention has shifted back to valuation targets, which point to higher implied upside for UnitedHealth than for Humana. Based on Koyfin estimates, UnitedHealth carries a 12-month average price target of $357.81, implying a 27% upside from the stock’s last close. Coverage across 29 analysts includes 7 ‘Strong Buy’, 16 ‘Buy’, 4 ‘Hold’ and 2 ‘Sell’ ratings. Earlier this month, Raymond James upgraded the stock to ‘Outperform’ with a $330 price target, citing potential upside from expense trends and expected margin improvement at Optum Health, the company’s care delivery arm. Meanwhile, Bernstein SocGen Group reiterated an ‘Outperform’ rating with a $405 target, pointing to UnitedHealth’s expanding AI strategy. The company recently launched its generative AI companion, Avery, as part of broader efforts to reduce operating costs across its insurance segment, where it plans nearly $1 billion in expense cuts and is closing or divesting about 550 Optum Health clinics. UnitedHealth also expects to lose as many as 2.8 million insurance members this year, with revenue potentially declining for the first time since the 1980s as longtime chair and former CEO Stephen Hemsley leads a turnaround effort. The stock still remains below the level at which Warren Buffett’s Berkshire Hathaway built its stake last year and faces scrutiny over Medicare Advantage risk-adjustment practices following a Senate committee review. Humana’s upside appears more modest based on Koyfin estimates, with a 12-month average price target of $212.17, implying a 16% upside from current levels. Among 27 covering analysts, the stock carries 2 ‘Strong Buy’, 6 ‘Buy’, 17 ‘Hold’ and 2 ‘Sell’ ratings. Earlier this year, the company projected adjusted 2026 earnings of at least $9 per share, below consensus expectations of $11.87, while the insurer said margins in its individual Medicare Advantage business could remain just below break-even this year. Several brokerages subsequently lowered price targets, with UBS and BofA maintaining ‘Neutral’ ratings after Humana’s 2026 EPS outlook came in roughly 24% below consensus. On the other hand, Morgan Stanley warned that uncertainty around the size of Humana’s 2026 membership cohort remains a risk “particularly heading into 2027 and beyond.” Cantor Fitzgerald said the stock may remain range-bound until clearer membership data emerges in the second quarter, and Guggenheim said it was taking “a prudent view” of the company’s 2027 earnings outlook. Still, Humana expects enrollment in its individual Medicare Advantage plans to increase about 25% in 2026 compared with last year, with over 70% of new members coming from competing plans. The U.S., Iran and regional mediators are reportedly exploring a possible 45-day ceasefire that could open the door to a settlement, while Washington and Tehran are also supposedly reviewing a Pakistan-brokered proposal to restore navigation through the Strait of Hormuz. However, Tehran has said it would only accept ceasefire terms that include a permanent end to the war, sanctions relief, reconstruction commitments and guarantees around safe navigation through the strait. It also warned that strikes on civilian infrastructure could trigger retaliatory attacks on energy facilities across the Gulf. The conflict, now in its sixth week, continues to ripple through energy markets, with West Texas Intermediate settling near $112.41 per barrel and Brent crude closing around $109.77. Michael Cembalest, chair of market and investment strategy at J.P. Morgan Asset & Wealth Management, said that the belief the U.S. economy is insulated from a closure of the Strait of Hormuz is “mostly false,” adding that U.S. fossil-fuel independence “is not as much of an economic firewall as you might think.” In the previous session, the S&P 500 logged its fourth straight session of gains, marking its longest winning streak since January: Investors also weighed weaker-than-expected economic data, with the U.S. services sector expanding at a slower pace in March. content: Get the best experience and stay connected to your community with our Spectrum News app. Learn More Get hyperlocal forecasts, radar and weather alerts. AUGUSTA — Another new poll on the race for U.S. Senate shows a statistical tie between Republican incumbent Sen. Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson. The University of New Hampshire Survey Center pegs Jackson at 51% and Collins at 47%, results the pollsters describe as essentially a tie because of the margin of error. And just like the New York Times/Portland Press Herald/Sienna survey released early Thursday, the UNH poll was in the field before a ProPublica story critical of Collins posted on Tuesday. That NYT poll shows Collins at 49% and Jackson at 46%. The UNH poll, conducted between Sept. 17-21, also asked voters about the race for governor, which features Democrat Hannah Pingree, Republican Bobby Charles and independent Rick Bennett. Results put Pingree at 48%, Charles at 40% and Bennett at 5%. Another interesting result comes from Maine voters’ views on outgoing Gov. Janet Mills, a Democrat finishing up her final year in office. The poll shows 57% disapproving of the way she handled the job as governor, 41% approving and 2% unsure. One of Mills’ key initiatives in the last year, issuing $300 “affordability checks” to many Mainers, also earned a lukewarm reception in the poll. Overall, 42% either somewhat or strongly support the program, 38% somewhat or strongly oppose it, with 14% offering no opinion. The payments were sent to single tax filers making up to $50,000 a year, $75,000 for head of household or $100,000 for married, filing jointly. The program cost about $155 million, with the money coming from the state’s Budget Stabilization Fund, also known as the rainy-day fund. Finally, UNH released new polling this week on President Donald Trump. It shows 62% of Maine residents disapprove of Trump’s overall job as president, 37% approve and 1 % are unsure. Second District Democrat Matt Dunlap says the federal government needs to do more to protect consumers. The comments came Wednesday at a town hall in Lewiston. title: UNH tradition goes up in smoke as Harvard triumphs - The New Hampshire
content: On Sept. 19, 2026, the University of New Hampshire’s Wildcat football team hosted the Harvard Crimson in Wildcat Stadium. Unfortunately for the home team, the Crimson were an astounding 17-point favorite. The Wildcats did an excellent job of shutting down the veteran Crimson offense in the first quarter. By the end of the first, the upset looked extremely promising. In addition to the hopeful win, the Wildcat fans got hyped for the annual chalk toss, held every year at the beginning of the Wildcat football season. The Cat Pack, made up of both students and alumni, have participated in this hype event for decades, and if tradition continues, hopefully many more to come. The chalk toss was initiated by the Cat Pack leaders, where they handed out handfuls of ‘chalk’ to the participants, waited for the countdown, and threw the smokey handfuls into the air to get pumped up for the game, to bring the UNH community together, and to bring victory to UNH. Shortly after however, the Wildcat’s hype train wore off quickly as the Crimson opened the second quarter with a 1-yard touchdown (TD). With their first redzone opportunity, the Wildcats stayed in the game with a rushing TD, but their fire went out quickly after the Harvard 20-yard option reverse touchdown, which extended their lead to 7. Shortly after, a brutal interception in their own territory in the final 20 seconds of the half brought the Crimson back into the redzone, which led to a two-score lead. The Wildcats headed back into the locker room, heads hung low, down 21-7. The Crimson got the ball after half, the Wildcat defence looked fierce and they forced the Crimson to either punt or try to go up another three. Fortunately for the Wildcats, the career-long field goal came up just short. The teams traded interceptions, ending in a Harvard field goal, which set the score 24-7. With defeat already in sight, the Wildcats went three-and-out which ultimately caused another Crimson TD. The teams traded possessions until Harvard took a knee, winning the game 31-7. Sadly, tradition wasn’t enough for the Wildcats to get the victory. Maybe next week the Wildcats can get the win when they travel to play Sacred Heart, who is currently 0-2.
